findings.title: import() calls are evaluated eagerly, so nothing is actually lazy-loaded
findings.body: The object literal calls `import("./applecalendar")`, `import("./caldavcalendar")`, … directly, which means every dynamic import is *started* the moment `packages/app-store/index.ts` is evaluated. The resulting object holds already-pending/resolved module promises, so all ~28 app packages (and their transitive deps such as googleapis, @microsoft/..., stripe, etc.) are still pulled into the bundle and executed at startup; the only thing that changed is that the consumer now has to `await` them. To get the intended benefit the map must hold thunks, e.g. `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`, and call sites must invoke them (`await appStore[key]()`). As written the PR adds async plumbing across the codebase without delivering the stated code-splitting/startup win.

findings.title: Eagerly created module promises can produce unhandled rejections and crash the process
findings.body: Because each `import(...)` promise is created at module-evaluation time and no `.catch()` is attached until (and unless) some code awaits that specific key, a module that throws while being evaluated (missing env var, bad app key parsing, native dep failure) produces a rejected promise with no handler. On Node >= 15 an unhandled rejection terminates the process by default, so one broken app package can take down the whole server even for requests that never touch that app. Previously a failing app module threw synchronously at import time of a single entry point and was at least deterministic/attributable. Storing lazy thunks (`() => import(...)`) avoids creating rejected promises nobody is listening to.

findings.title: getCalendarCredentials now returns a Promise in its `calendar` field (silent contract change + floating promise)
findings.body: `getCalendarCredentials` stays synchronous but `getCalendar(credential)` is now async, so each returned item's `calendar` property is a `Promise<Calendar | null>` instead of a `Calendar | null`. `getConnectedCalendars` was updated to `await item.calendar`, but any other consumer of `getCalendarCredentials` (it is a public export of @calcom/core) that reads `.calendar` now receives a promise and will silently misbehave (e.g. truthiness checks always pass, method calls throw). Additionally, these promises are created and left unhandled inside `flatMap`: if a credential's app module fails to load, the rejection has no handler attached, giving an unhandled rejection. Consider making `getCalendarCredentials` async and resolving the calendars (with per-item error handling) before returning.

findings.title: Recurring-booking calendar deletions are pushed into apiDeletes after it is already awaited
findings.body: In the recurring branch, `bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(...).forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent) })` uses an async callback inside `forEach`, so the callbacks return immediately and the `apiDeletes.push(...)` happens on later microtasks. By the time `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` runs at the end of the handler, `apiDeletes` is still empty, so the remote calendar events for the remaining recurring occurrences are deleted fire-and-forget (and their failures surface as unhandled rejections rather than being reported). The sibling non-credentialId branch in this same diff was correctly converted to a `for...of` loop; this branch should be too (e.g. `for (const credential of ...)` with awaited deletes pushed as promises).

findings.title: requestReschedule fires calendar/video cancellations without awaiting them
findings.body: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...) ... })` makes every iteration an un-awaited async task. The tRPC mutation then proceeds to send the reschedule email and returns while the external calendar `deleteEvent` / `deleteMeeting` calls may not have started (they now need at least one extra microtask to resolve the dynamic app import). In a serverless/edge deployment the function can be frozen or torn down before the deletions run, leaving stale events on the user's calendar, and any rejection becomes an unhandled promise rejection. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (ref) => ...))` so the work completes (and errors are caught) before responding.

findings.title: try/catch around forEach(async ...) cannot catch anything and deletions are not awaited
findings.body: Converting the `forEach` callback to `async` means `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); ... })` returns before any deletion happens, so the surrounding `try { ... } catch (error) { logger.error(...) }` can never observe a failure — rejections escape as unhandled promise rejections instead of being logged. The function also proceeds to send the reschedule email and `return true` while the external calendar/video cancellations may not have executed. Replace with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (ref) => ...))` inside the try block.

findings.title: try/catch around forEach(async ...) cannot catch anything and deletions are not awaited
findings.body: Same defect as in the vital app: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { await getCalendar(...) ... })` returns immediately, so the enclosing `try/catch` that logs errors is dead code and any failure of `calendar.deleteEvent` / `deleteMeeting` becomes an unhandled rejection. The reschedule email is sent and `true` returned before the external cancellations are known to have completed, which can leave orphaned calendar/video events. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(...))` so the awaited work is covered by the try/catch.
